transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. Um, so I just finished my bachelor's recently, and I've been in this weird limbo phase, you know, trying to figure out what's next, applying for things... and what finally made me actually pick up the phone and make this appointment—because I've been thinking about it for a while, honestly—but what finally did it is that I just keep... I keep turning in these applications, or like, my research notes, with these really small but just incredibly embarrassing mistakes. 

Like, for example, I was doing this write-up recently and I completely mislabeled an artwork date. Which is just... it's so bad, especially when you're trying to look professional. Or I'll be filling out a long application form and I'll just completely skip a question entirely. And the crazy part is, I swear to you, I check them. Like, I will sit there and read over the document, and I honestly think I've checked everything perfectly, I really do, and then I hit submit. And then later I look back and the mistake is just sitting right there glaring at me. 

It's just so frustrating because I'm not stupid, you know? But it keeps happening and it makes me look so careless to these places I'm applying to, and I just don't know why my brain skips right over these details even when I'm staring right at them. So, yeah, I just really need to figure out what's going wrong there because it's starting to really mess with my confidence.
Did you have similar trouble paying attention or making careless mistakes when you were a child?

Yeah, actually, I did. It’s funny you ask that because I was just talking to my mom about this the other day, and she brought out this old box of my report cards from when I was a kid. Like, we’re talking second, third grade, all the way through elementary school. And it was wild reading through them because it’s the exact same stuff I’m dealing with now, just, you know, a kid version of it. 

Every single teacher would write these comments—and I mean almost word for word the same thing every year—they’d say I was a sweet kid, that I had really good ideas, or that I was creative, but then there was always the "but." It was always, "but he forgets to turn in his worksheets," or "he loses the instructions for the project before he even gets home." I remember this one time in fourth grade, we had this big diorama project, and I was so excited about it, I spent all weekend thinking about how I was going to build it, but I had completely lost the rubric, so I missed like half the requirements. 

And the little details, too, just like now. I’d do a whole math worksheet and just skip an entire row of problems. Not because I didn't know how to do them, I just literally didn't see them. My parents actually had to start this whole system where they would sit down with me every single night and physically unpack my backpack, folder by folder, just to make sure I hadn't missed anything or stuffed a permission slip at the bottom where it would get crumpled up. If they didn't do that, things just... disappeared. Or I'd do the homework and then leave it sitting on the kitchen counter the next morning. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing, it’s just... the stakes are a lot higher now than missing a spelling test, you know?
Do you also have trouble understanding what you read?

Um, no, actually. Not at all. That's the weird thing, right? Because you'd think if I'm missing all these details, maybe I just don't get the material. But I actually completely understand what I'm reading. 

Like, for my degree, I had to read these massive, incredibly dense academic papers—especially for my upper-level seminars. And I could sit down and read a fifty-page text on, I don't know, some really heavy theoretical framework, and I could completely grasp the overarching concepts. I'd actually be the one in the seminar leading the discussion on the themes and the author's main arguments, because I really get the big picture stuff. So the comprehension part is totally fine. I process the actual meaning perfectly. 

It's just... well, if you asked me to remember the exact year the author cited on page twelve, or if I had to copy over a specific quote without missing a word, that's where things fall apart. But the actual understanding of the text? No, I've never really struggled with that at all. Which honestly just makes it even more baffling to me, you know? Because my brain clearly works when it comes to understanding really complex stuff, so why can't I just read a basic application form without my eyes skipping over an entire question? It just feels like such a disconnect between what I know I can understand and what I actually manage to output.
When you read, do you ever have trouble recognizing or decoding the words themselves?

No, no, nothing like that. The words themselves are totally fine. I mean, I don't look at a page and see the letters jumbled up or backwards or anything like that. I know some people have that, like dyslexia, right? Where the words kind of swim around on the page or they have to really sound things out even when they're older. But for me, reading the actual words has always been super easy. 

Actually, I was one of those kids who learned to read really early, like before kindergarten even, and I was always way ahead in reading level. I'd just tear through books. My mom used to joke that she couldn't keep enough books in the house because I'd finish them so fast. I never had to sit there and struggle to sound out syllables or figure out what a word was supposed to be. The mechanics of reading, like the actual decoding part, that's completely automatic for me. 

It's really just... it's the attention part, I guess. Like I said, I'll be reading along, completely understanding the words, decoding them perfectly, and then suddenly I realize my eyes have just glazed over a whole paragraph, or I've skipped a line without even noticing, or I've read the same sentence three times because my brain was somewhere else entirely. But the letters and the words themselves? They stay exactly where they're supposed to be. I just... I don't know, I just don't always process the little details in them, even though I can read them perfectly fine. It's so weird to explain, honestly, because it sounds like a contradiction, but the decoding part is definitely not the issue.
When you need to focus on something, do you often find your mind drifting off even when you’re trying not to?

Yeah, oh my gosh, all the time. It’s honestly one of the most frustrating things because I’ll sit down with every intention of getting something done. Like, I’ll be at my desk, right? I’ve got my coffee, I’ve got my laptop open, I’ve told myself, "Okay, we are going to read this article or write this section of the paper," and I’m really trying to focus. I’m putting in the effort. 

But then, I don't know, a siren will go off outside down the street, and suddenly my brain is completely hijacked by that sound. Or I’ll hear someone talking out in the hallway—not even a loud conversation, just a murmur—and my focus just snaps right to it. And it doesn't even have to be an external noise, either. That's the crazy part. Sometimes it’s just my own brain betraying me. I’ll be reading along, and a word will trigger a completely random thought. Like, I’ll be reading about art history, and suddenly I’m thinking about an idea I had for an exhibit, and how I would arrange the lighting, and what pieces I’d put together, and what the brochure would look like... 

And before I even realize what’s happening, like, twenty minutes have gone by. Twenty whole minutes where I haven't read a single word or typed a single sentence because my mind just went on this massive detour. And it’s not like I chose to stop working. I didn't say, "Let me take a break and think about this exhibit." It just happens. And then I have to sort of snap myself back to reality and figure out where I even left off, which takes another five minutes just to reorient myself. It’s exhausting, honestly, because it feels like I’m constantly fighting my own brain just to stay on one track, and the slightest little thing—inside or outside—just derails the whole train.
Do these attention slips happen in other parts of your life too, like conversations, chores, or everyday errands?

Yeah, oh, absolutely. It's not just when I'm trying to sit down and work, it bleeds into literally everything else. It's actually incredibly embarrassing sometimes. Like, I’ll mean to do just normal, everyday adult things, right? The kind of stuff everyone else seems to just do without thinking. I'll get an email, maybe from a professor or even just a friend asking a simple question, and I'll look at it, read it, and think, "Okay, I need to check my calendar before I reply, I'll do that right after I finish making this sandwich." And then... it's just gone. It completely evaporates from my brain. 

And it's not just emails. It's paying bills, too. I'll get the notification on my phone, I'll swipe it away thinking, "I'll log into the portal tonight," and then three weeks later I'm getting a late notice and kicking myself because I actually had the money sitting in my account, I just literally forgot the task existed. Or groceries! Oh man, the groceries. I'll go to the kitchen, realize we're out of milk, and tell myself, "Pick up milk on the way home today." I won't write it down because I think, "It's just milk, how could I forget milk?" And then I'll walk right past the grocery store, get all the way home, take my shoes off, and realize I never did it. 

It just drops out of my mind completely. Like there's a hole in my pocket and the thought just slipped right through. And then days later, or when it's too late, it'll suddenly pop back in, and I'm left scrambling or apologizing again. It makes me feel so flaky, you know? Like I'm unreliable, even though my intention is always to do these things right away. I just... I get distracted by whatever is right in front of me, and the thing I was supposed to hold onto just vanishes.
